Question: How many whole numbers between \(100\) and \(400\) contain the digit \(2?\)
Solution:
Method 1: Count disjoint digit cases

Neither \(100\) nor \(400\) contains a \(2\), so including or excluding the endpoints makes no difference. Count the numbers from \(100\) through \(399\) by their hundreds digit.

Every number from \(200\) through \(299\) qualifies. There are \(10\) choices for each of its last two digits, giving \(10\cdot10=100\) numbers.

For each hundreds digit \(1\) or \(3\), there are \(10\) qualifying numbers with tens digit \(2\). There are also \(9\) with ones digit \(2\) and tens digit different from \(2\). This restriction keeps numbers such as \(122\) and \(322\) from being counted twice. These two groups cover every way a number in either block can contain a \(2\).

The hundreds-digit cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so the total is
\[
100+2(10+9)=138.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{138}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

Method 2: Subtract the numbers with no 2

It is easier to count numbers with no digit \(2\), because each digit then has a simple restriction. Neither endpoint \(100\) nor \(400\) contains a \(2\), so we may count within the \(300\) numbers from \(100\) through \(399\).

A number in this range with no \(2\) has \(2\) choices for its hundreds digit, namely \(1\) or \(3\). Its tens and ones digits each have \(9\) choices: any digit except \(2\). Each combination gives exactly one number, so there are
\[
2\cdot9\cdot9=162
\]
numbers with no \(2\). Every number either contains a \(2\) or contains none, so the desired count is
\[
300-162=138.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{138}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
